front_blocks.md: Define **contrast** in X-ray imaging.

back_blocks.md: **Contrast** is the difference in the degree of blackening between structures.

cards.front_md: Define **contrast** in X-ray imaging.

front_blocks.md: Define **sharpness** in X-ray imaging.

back_blocks.md: **Sharpness** is how well-defined the edges of structures are.

cards.front_md: Define **sharpness** in X-ray imaging.
cards.back_md: **Sharpness** is how well-defined the edges of structures are.

front_blocks.md: How are X-ray photons produced in an X-ray tube?

back_blocks.md: Electrons released by **thermionic emission** at the cathode are accelerated towards the anode; when they bombard the metal target, they rapidly decelerate and transfer their kinetic energy into **X-ray photons**.

cards.front_md: How are X-ray photons produced in an X-ray tube?
cards.back_md: Electrons released by **thermionic emission** at the cathode are accelerated towards the anode; when they bombard the metal target, they rapidly decelerate and transfer their kinetic energy into **X-ray photons**.

front_blocks.md: State the equation for the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced by an accelerating voltage *V*.

back_blocks.md: $λ_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}$

cards.front_md: State the equation for the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced by an accelerating voltage *V*.
cards.back_md: $λ_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}$

front_blocks.md: Why does the X-ray spectrum have a sharp cut-off at short wavelengths?

back_blocks.md: At the cut-off, each electron gives up **all** its kinetic energy in a single collision to produce one photon, corresponding to the **maximum** possible photon energy and so the **minimum** wavelength.

cards.front_md: Why does the X-ray spectrum have a sharp cut-off at short wavelengths?
cards.back_md: At the cut-off, each electron gives up **all** its kinetic energy in a single collision to produce one photon, corresponding to the **maximum** possible photon energy and so the **minimum** wavelength.

front_blocks.md: Why are aluminium filters used in medical X-ray imaging?

back_blocks.md: They **absorb** long-wavelength (soft) X-rays, which are less penetrating and more likely to be absorbed by the body without contributing to the image, reducing patient radiation dose.

front_blocks.md: Image sharpness can be improved by using a narrower X-ray beam and reducing scattering with a **..........** or lead grid.

back_blocks.md: Image sharpness can be improved by using a narrower X-ray beam and reducing scattering with a **collimator** or lead grid.

cards.front_md: Image sharpness can be improved by using a narrower X-ray beam and reducing scattering with a **..........** or lead grid.
cards.back_md: Image sharpness can be improved by using a narrower X-ray beam and reducing scattering with a **collimator** or lead grid.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Harder (higher energy) X-rays always give better image contrast, whatever tissue is being imaged.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
**Hard X-rays** are used for imaging bone and **soft X-rays** for tissue; the correct level of hardness depends on the structure being imaged.

front_blocks.md: Define **attenuation** of an X-ray beam.

back_blocks.md: **Attenuation** is the reduction in the intensity of an X-ray beam as it passes through matter.

cards.front_md: Define **attenuation** of an X-ray beam.
cards.back_md: **Attenuation** is the reduction in the intensity of an X-ray beam as it passes through matter.

front_blocks.md: Why do bones appear white on an X-ray photograph?

back_blocks.md: **Bones absorb** X-ray radiation strongly, so little radiation passes through to reach the detector or film at that point.

cards.front_md: Why do bones appear white on an X-ray photograph?
cards.back_md: **Bones absorb** X-ray radiation strongly, so little radiation passes through to reach the detector or film at that point.

front_blocks.md: State the equation for the attenuation of X-rays in matter, and give the meaning of each symbol.

back_blocks.md:
- *I*<sub>0</sub> = intensity of the incident beam
- *I* = intensity of the emergent beam
- *μ* = linear absorption coefficient
- *x* = distance travelled through the material

cards.front_md: State the equation for the attenuation of X-rays in matter, and give the meaning of each symbol.
cards.back_md:
$I = I_{0} e^{-μx}$

- *I*<sub>0</sub> = intensity of the incident beam
- *I* = intensity of the emergent beam
- *μ* = linear absorption coefficient
- *x* = distance travelled through the material

front_blocks.md: Define **half thickness**.

back_blocks.md: The **half thickness** is the thickness of material that reduces the intensity of an X-ray beam of a particular frequency to half its original value.

cards.back_md: The **half thickness** is the thickness of material that reduces the intensity of an X-ray beam of a particular frequency to half its original value.

front_blocks.md: As an X-ray beam passes through matter, its intensity decreases **..........** with distance travelled.

back_blocks.md: As an X-ray beam passes through matter, its intensity decreases **exponentially** with distance travelled.

front_blocks.md: What two processes remove photons from an X-ray beam as it passes through the body?

back_blocks.md:
- **Absorption**
- **Scattering**

front_blocks.md: What condition on the intensity ratio *I*/*I*<sub>0</sub> indicates good contrast between two tissues?

back_blocks.md: There is a large difference between the intensities, so the ratio *I*/*I*<sub>0</sub> is **much less than 1.0**.

cards.back_md: There is a large difference between the intensities, so the ratio *I*/*I*<sub>0</sub> is **much less than 1.0**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The linear absorption coefficient, *μ*, is the same for X-ray photons of any energy.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The linear absorption coefficient **depends on the energy of the X-ray photons**, as well as the material.

front_blocks.md: Define a **computed tomography (CT) scan**.

back_blocks.md: A **CT scan** is an imaging technique in which an X-ray tube rotates around a stationary patient, taking X-ray images of the same slice at many different angles, which a computer combines to build a 3D image.

cards.front_md: Define a **computed tomography (CT) scan**.
cards.back_md: A **CT scan** is an imaging technique in which an X-ray tube rotates around a stationary patient, taking X-ray images of the same slice at many different angles, which a computer combines to build a 3D image.

front_blocks.md: How is a 3D image built up during a CT scan?

back_blocks.md:
- X-ray images of the **same slice** are taken at many different angles
- This process is **repeated** for successive slices
- A computer **combines** the slice images together to build a **3D image**, which can be rotated and viewed from different angles

cards.front_md: How is a 3D image built up during a CT scan?
cards.back_md:
- X-ray images of the **same slice** are taken at many different angles
- This process is **repeated** for successive slices
- A computer **combines** the slice images together to build a **3D image**, which can be rotated and viewed from different angles

front_blocks.md: State three advantages of a CT scan compared with a single X-ray image.

back_blocks.md:
- Produces images of much **higher resolution**
- Can **distinguish between tissues** with similar attenuation coefficients
- Produces a **3D image** of the body

front_blocks.md: State two disadvantages of a CT scan compared with a single X-ray image.

back_blocks.md:
- The patient receives a much **higher radiation dose**
- There are **possible side effects** from the contrast media used

A CT scan produces only a single 2D image of the body.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
A CT scan combines many 2D images, taken of successive slices from multiple angles, to build up a single **3D image**.
